title: Connecting to OBS
content: Turn your Cables.gl patch into an OBS controller without browser sandbox restrictions. Because Cables patches often run within an <iframe> or under strict browser origin sandboxing, establishing direct local WebSocket connections to 127.0.0.1:4455 can trigger security blocks or CORS issues. Enter Ops.Team.CablesStudio.Externals.ExternalObsConnection: an op that establishes a reliable, bidirectional link between your Cables patch and OBS Studio using a dedicated top-level popup bridge and the native browser BroadcastChannel API. Here is a how it works and how to set it up in your own patches! What is ExternalObsConnection Op? ExternalObsConnection is a specialized op designed to connect Cables directly to OBS Studio via WebSocket v5. Instead of fighting sandbox and mixed-content limitations inside the Cables canvas frame, the op launches a sleek external popup bridge. That popup lives as a top-level window, connects directly to OBS Studio over local WebSocket (ws://127.0.0.1:4455), and mirrors commands and broadcast events back and forth using the high-performance browser BroadcastChannel API. Why Use It? Zero Sandbox Headaches: Bypasses iframe restrictions cleanly without requiring custom browser flags or insecure workarounds. Full OBS WebSocket v5 Power: Control scenes, toggle sources, adjust audio filters, trigger transitions, start/stop streams, and query status. Smart Request Handling: Supports canonical OBS payload formats, flat convenience objects, and multi-command batch arrays. Automated Rate-Limiting & Batching: Set a throttling rate (Request Rate (Hz)) to automatically bundle rapid slider or fader events into a single WebSocket RequestBatch, preventing socket congestion and race conditions. Live Bidirectional Events: Listen for real-time OBS state changes (e.g. CurrentProgramSceneChanged, InputMuteStateChanged) and feed them directly into your Cables animations. Built-in Visual Diagnostic Bridge: The popup window displays real-time connection status badges, host addresses, and live event/request logs so you always know what is happening under the hood. How the Pieces Fit Together Here is a look at the data flow between Cables, your browser, and OBS Studio: ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Your Browser │ │ │ │ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Cables.gl Patch │ │ │ │ (Inside Iframe) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ExternalObsConnection │ │ │ └───────────┬────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ BroadcastChannel │ │ │ ("obs-external-bridge") │ │ ▼ │ │ ┌────────────────────────┐ Local WebSocket │ │ │ Popup Bridge Window │ ◄────────────────────────► │ │ │ (Top-Level Context) │ ws://127.0.0.1:4455 │ │ └────────────────────────┘ │ └────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────┐ │ OBS Studio │ │ (WebSocket v5) │ │ - Scenes │ │ - Audio Mixer │ │ - Transitions │ └───────────────────┘ Step-by-Step Setup Guide Step 1: Enable the WebSocket Server in OBS Studio Before touching Cables, ensure OBS Studio is ready to accept WebSocket connections: Open OBS Studio (v28 or newer, which includes WebSocket v5 natively). Go to Tools > WebSocket Server Settings. Check Enable WebSocket server. Check or configure the Server Port (default is 4455). (Optional but recommended) Enable authentication and enter a Server Password. Click Apply and OK. Step 2: Add the Op to Your Cables Patch In the Cables editor, press Escape or double-click to open the Op selector. Search for and place: Ops.Team.CablesStudio.Externals.ExternalObsConnection Set your connection parameters in the op inspector: Host / URL: 127.0.0.1 (or your OBS machine's IP address) Port: 4455 Password: Enter the password set in OBS (leave blank if authentication is disabled) Broadcast Channel Name: Keep as obs-external-bridge (or give it a unique name if running multiple patches) Step 3: Open the Popup Bridge Click the Open Popup button in the op inspector (or trigger it with an op like Button or Once). Tip on Popups: Browsers will typically block popups that open automatically on page load. Triggering Open Popup via a user interaction (like clicking a button in your patch) ensures your browser permits the popup window without warnings. Once opened, the popup bridge window will open with a dark diagnostic interface. It connects to OBS and displays a glowing green Connected badge, confirming that Cables and OBS are linked. Sending Commands to OBS The Request Data input accepts clean JSON objects. Updating Request Data automatically sends the request, or you can trigger Send Request manually. 1. Canonical OBS Request You can pass the standard OBS WebSocket v5 structure: { "requestType": "GetSceneList", "requestData": {} } 2. Convenient Flat Parameters For quick setup, you can place parameters directly at the top level without nesting requestData: { "requestType": "SetCurrentProgramScene", "sceneName": "Camera 1" } 3. Direct Batch Requests Want to execute multiple operations at once? Pass an array into Request Data: [ { "requestType": "SetCurrentProgramScene", "requestData": { "sceneName": "Main Presentation" } }, { "requestType": "SetInputMute", "requestData": { "inputName": "Microphone", "inputMuted": false } } ] Automatic Rate Limiting & Throttling When binding Cables UI sliders, MIDI faders, or mouse coordinates to OBS properties (like volume or filter settings), you might produce dozens or hundreds of events every second. Firing individual network requests at high frequency can overwhelm the WebSocket connection. ExternalObsConnection includes an intelligent batching system: Set Request Rate (Hz) to a non-zero value (e.g. 10 Hz or 20 Hz). Any requests triggered within that time window (1000 / Rate ms) are automatically bundled into a single OBS WebSocket RequestBatch. When OBS returns the batch results, the op automatically demultiplexes the response and triggers On Response sequentially for each transaction. Reacting to Live OBS Events Communication isn't just one-way! When you switch scenes or adjust volume in OBS, ExternalObsConnection captures those events in real time. Connect the On Event output trigger to your patch logic. Read Event Name (e.g., CurrentProgramSceneChanged, InputMuteStateChanged, or RecordStateChanged). Inspect Event Data to extract payloads such as the active scene name or volume levels. Use subscriptions in the op inspector (e.g., Sub Scenes, Sub Inputs, Sub Volume Meters) to toggle which event categories you want to receive. Summary of Ports | Port Name | Direction | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Host / URL | Input | IP or hostname of the OBS WebSocket server (default: 127.0.0.1). | | Port | Input | Port number of the server (default: 4455). | | Password | Input | WebSocket authentication password. | | Open / Close Popup | Input | Buttons to open or dismiss the external bridge window. | | Request Rate (Hz) | Input | Automated batching frequency (0 = immediate execution). | | Request Data | Input | Payload object or array describing the OBS command. | | Connected | Output | Boolean indicating if the bridge is currently connected to OBS. | | On Response | Output | Triggered whenever a command returns its response. | | Response Data | Output | The response payload returned by OBS. | | On Event | Output | Triggered when OBS broadcasts an event. | | Event Name | Output | Name of the emitted event (e.g., CurrentProgramSceneChanged). | | Error | Output | String containing error messages if a connection or request fails. | Wrapping Up With ExternalObsConnection, Cables becomes an interactive command center for your stream. Whether you're building interactive stream overlays that react to scene changes, generative VJ visuals triggered by OBS hotkeys, or custom browser-based remote control surfaces, you can now link Cables and OBS Studio with ease. Happy patching!

title: Publishing Slides
content: If you love Obsidian as your digital brain, you already know the power of connecting your thoughts. But sometimes a flat wall of text doesn't cut it. When you need to explain an architecture, deliver a tutorial, or summarize key takeaways, slides just work better. By combining Slides Extended with the Digital Garden plugin and a touch of VS Code, you can publish interactive, keyboard-navigable slide decks embedded directly inside your public notes on GitHub Pages. Here is the complete, update-safe guide to setting up this workflow. What is Slides Extended? Slides Extended is an Obsidian community plugin that turns Markdown notes into presentations powered by Reveal.js. Place a horizontal rule (---) between your sections, and Obsidian renders a full slide presentation with speaker notes, animations, side-by-side layouts, and custom themes. Why Embed Slides in Your Digital Garden? Dual-Format Consumption: Visual learners can click through your slides, while deep-divers can scroll down to read the longform notes on the same page. Interactive Polish: It elevates your garden beyond static prose, giving your documentation or portfolio a dynamic feel. No Third-Party Hosting: Keep your presentation assets in your own GitHub repository without relying on external services like Google Slides or SlideShare. How the Pieces Fit Together The Digital Garden plugin publishes Markdown notes to GitHub via the GitHub API, but it doesn't bundle complex multi-file HTML slide folders. By cloning your site repository in VS Code, you can easily drop the exported slides into your repository, configure an update-safe passthrough rule in Eleventy, and push everything via VS Code's Source Control panel. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Your Local Machine │ │ │ │ ┌──────────────────────┐ Export HTML │ │ │ Obsidian Vault │ ─────────────────┐ │ │ │ (Slide Note & Iframe)│ │ │ │ └──────────┬───────────┘ ▼ │ │ │ ┌────────────────┐ │ │ │ DG Plugin │ Exported Deck │ │ │ │ (Note Only) │ (index + dist) │ │ │ │ └───────┬────────┘ │ │ │ │ Drag & drop│ │ │ ▼ in VS Code │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ Local Repo Clone │ │ │ │ │ (Opened in VS Code│ │ │ │ └─────────┬─────────┘ │ └─────────────┼─────────────────────────────┼────────────┘ │ │ VS Code Sync │ │ (git push) │ ▼ ┌─────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ▼ GitHub │ │ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Digital Garden Repository │ │ │ │ - Notes: /src/site/notes/ │ │ │ │ - Slides: /src/site/slides/<deck-name>/ │ │ │ │ - Passthrough: src/helpers/userSetup.js │ │ │ └───────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ (Eleventy Build) │ │ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ GitHub Pages │ │ │ │ https://<username>.github.io/<repo>/slides/...│ │ │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Step 1: Export Your Slides to HTML Open your slide note in Obsidian. Press Cmd + P (macOS) or Ctrl + P (Windows/Linux) to open the Command Palette. Select: Slides Extended: Export presentation to HTML Choose an export destination (such as your Downloads folder). Name the export folder using clean URL slugging with no spaces (e.g., system-architecture). This creates a folder containing index.html alongside Reveal.js support folders (dist/, plugin/, css/). Step 2: Clone Your Garden Repo in VS Code Using VS Code handles authentication and folder management without needing terminal commands. Open VS Code. Press Cmd + Shift + P (or Ctrl + Shift + P) to open the Command Palette. Type and run: Git: Clone Paste the URL of your Digital Garden GitHub repository (e.g., [https://github.com/](https://github.com/)<your-username>/<your-garden-repo>.git) and press Enter. Select a local directory to save the repository, then click Open when prompted. If asked, sign in with your GitHub account so VS Code manages your credentials automatically. Step 3: Configure Passthrough in userSetup.js By default, the Eleventy engine that powers Digital Garden only copies specific recognized assets into the final production build. Digital Garden provides src/helpers/userSetup.js as a permanent, update-safe hook to customize the build configuration without getting overwritten by template updates. In VS Code's file explorer, open: src/helpers/userSetup.js Add eleventyConfig.addPassthroughCopy("src/site/slides"); inside userEleventySetup: function userMarkdownSetup(md) { // The md parameter stands for the markdown-it instance used throughout the site generator. // Feel free to add any plugin you want here instead of /.eleventy.js } function userEleventySetup(eleventyConfig) { // The eleventyConfig parameter stands for the the config instantiated in /.eleventy.js. // Feel free to add any plugin you want here instead of /.eleventy.js // Copy all slide decks and their assets verbatim into dist/slides/ eleventyConfig.addPassthroughCopy("src/site/slides"); } exports.userMarkdownSetup = userMarkdownSetup; exports.userEleventySetup = userEleventySetup; Save the file (Cmd + S or Ctrl + S). Step 4: Copy the Slides and Push via VS Code In VS Code's file tree, create a slides folder under src/site/ if it doesn't already exist: src/site/slides/ Drag and drop your exported presentation folder (e.g., system-architecture) from your file manager directly into src/site/slides/ inside VS Code. Make sure the path looks like: src/site/slides/system-architecture/index.html. Switch to the Source Control tab on the left sidebar (or press Ctrl + Shift + G). Type a commit message (e.g., "Add system-architecture slides and passthrough rule"). Click Commit, then click Sync Changes (or Push). Once the GitHub Actions build finishes on your repository, the slides will be live at: https://<your-username>.github.io/<repo-name>/slides/system-architecture/ Step 5: Embed the Slides in an Obsidian Note Back in Obsidian, create or open the note that will display your slides to garden visitors. Add your frontmatter and a responsive <iframe>: --- dg-publish: true title: "System Architecture Walkthrough" tags: - architecture - slides --- # Architecture Overview Use the controls below or keyboard arrow keys to navigate the presentation: <div style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden; max-width: 100%; border-radius: 8px; border: 1px solid #333; margin: 1.5rem 0;"> <iframe src="/<repo-name>/slides/system-architecture/" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border: 0;" allowfullscreen="true"> </iframe> </div> [Open presentation in a new tab](/<repo-name>/slides/system-architecture/) --- ## Accompanying Notes Here are the detailed references and background context for the slides above... Path Note: If your site is hosted on GitHub Pages under a repository subpath (e.g., username.github.io/my-garden/), include your repository name prefix: /<repo-name>/slides/<deck-name>/. If you use a custom domain (e.g., notes.yourdomain.com), use the root path: /slides/<deck-name>/. Step 6: Publish Your Note In Obsidian, open the Command Palette (Cmd + P or Ctrl + P). Run: Digital Garden: Publish Active Note Digital Garden commits the Markdown note to GitHub via the API, triggering Eleventy to rebuild the site. Your readers will now see an interactive, full-screen Reveal.js presentation embedded within your published garden note. Slides Extended Example Open Presentation Fullscreen Slides.com Example Slides.com is a visual interface for Reveal.js slides. Marimo Slides Example Marimo is a python notebook analysis tool that can export interactive Reveal.js slides. These slides can be copied to the local digital garden folder and embedded in notes.
